title: Plans & Invitations
description: Suggesting, arranging and gently turning down plans with friends, from 'are you free on Saturday?' to 'I'm on my way'. Where a line is casual, the standard version comes with it.

phrases.english: Are you doing anything this Saturday?
phrases.registerNotes: The usual way to check someone is free before inviting them: literally 'is there an event this Saturday'. Friends add nggak at the end: Sabtu ini ada acara, nggak?

phrases.english: How about going to the beach?
phrases.registerNotes: Bagaimana kalau … is the standard 'how about …' for any suggestion. Friends say Gimana kalau …, or just Ke pantai, yuk.
phrases.pitfallNote: Use kita, which includes the person you're inviting; kami would leave them out.

phrases.registerNotes: Yuk is the friendly, casual 'let's', and it usually comes last: Makan, yuk. Ngopi is spoken for minum kopi, and often just means meeting up for a chat.

phrases.indonesian: Kita ketemu di depan stasiun, ya.
phrases.english: Let's meet in front of the station, OK?

polite.indonesian: Kita bertemu di depan stasiun, ya.

phrases.registerNotes: Ketemu is the everyday spoken bertemu; bertemu sounds more careful and suits work or older people. The ya at the end checks the other person is happy with it.
Enaknya, 'what would be nice', hands the choice to the other person: Enaknya di mana? (Where's good for you?). Polite with anyone.
Boleh, literally 'may', is the everyday yes to a suggestion or an offer. Boleh juga is a slightly less certain 'why not'.

phrases.indonesian: Maaf, saya tidak bisa. Ada acara keluarga.
phrases.english: Sorry, I can't. I've got a family thing on.
phrases.registerNotes: Friends say Sori, nggak bisa. Ada acara keluarga.
phrases.cultureNote: A bare no feels abrupt in Indonesian, so people give a reason, and a family event is one nobody argues with.

phrases.registerNotes: A gentle no, or putting something off, said with a smile.
phrases.cultureNote: From an Indonesian friend it may well mean no rather than 'ask me again next week'; read it with the tone and the reason given.

phrases.registerNotes: From kabar (news): 'I'll send word'. Friends say Nanti aku kabarin.
phrases.cultureNote: Like lain kali, it can also be a polite way of not committing.

phrases.registerNotes: Lagi is casual for sedang (in the middle of). In messages people just write otw, said o-te-we, from English 'on the way'.
phrases.pitfallNote: Di jalan can mean anything from 'just leaving' to 'nearly there'. Sudah dekat? (Are you close?) is a fair follow-up.

phrases.english: Sorry, I'm running a bit late.
phrases.registerNotes: Telat is the spoken terlambat: to a friend, Sori, telat dikit, ya.
phrases.cultureNote: Indonesians joke about jam karet, 'rubber time'. Friends allow some leeway, but be on time for work, appointments and older people.

phrases.english: We're still on for tomorrow, right?
phrases.registerNotes: Said the day before, to confirm a plan. Besok jadi? on its own is the casual version.
phrases.pitfallNote: Jadi here means 'goes ahead as planned', not 'so'. Tidak jadi, or nggak jadi among friends, means it's off.

phrases.registerNotes: Jemput is to go and collect someone. The other half is antar, to take someone somewhere: Saya antar pulang, ya? (Shall I take you home?)
